title: Enterprise Architecture for Power Platform Management
summary: Your Power Platform isn’t breaking because of “bad code”—it’s the invisible feedback loops between environments, DLP, connectors, and ALM that trigger domino failures. This guide shows how a tiny governance tweak in Dev/Test can stall pipelines in Prod, and gives you a practical blueprint to map, monitor, and break those loops: cloneable environments, policy tiers, connector parity, variable governance, and pre-flight ALM checks that catch drift before it explodes.
show_notes: Most “random” release failures aren’t random: they’re feedback loops created by environment drift + DLP/connector changes + incomplete ALM assumptions. Design environments as a system : standardize policy tiers, enforce connector parity, govern environment variables, and add pre-flight ALM checks to catch drift before production. 🧭 The Problem in One Picture (Mental Model) Dev ↔ Test ↔ Prod aren’t boxes—they’re a network of gates (DLP policies, connectors, roles, env vars, licenses, CA rules). Nudge any gate and the wave hits your pipelines elsewhere (validation, connection refs, solution imports). Fixes at the pipeline layer won’t stick if the environment layer is drifting. 🚨 Classic Domino Scenarios (Recognize These?) “Safe” DLP tweak in Dev/Test → Solution validation fails (blocked HTTP connector needed for packaging/validation). Connector mix-and-match in non-prod → Prod lacks the same connector SKU/region → flows 401/403 post-deploy. Forgotten environment variable used only in Dev → pipeline promotes null values → Prod emails/approvals fail. Conditional Access/preview features allowed in Dev → blocked in Prod → makers can’t edit or re-auth connections. Licensing drift (capacity add-ons only in Prod) → works in Staging, falls over live. ✅ Design Principles that Prevent Domino Effects Policy Tiers, Not One-Offs: Tier 0 (Sandbox) : permissive for maker speed; heavy telemetry. Tier 1 (Test) : mirror Prod DLP + CA; no preview. Tier 2 (Prod) : locked; approved connectors only; change via CAB. Connector Parity Contracts: same connector types, regions, SKUs, auth models across Dev/Test/Prod; no previews outside Tier 0. Environment Variable Governance: all required env vars defined with default + per-environment values stored in repo; no hard-coded fallbacks. Role & Identity Symmetry: service principals + connection references created identically in every environment; PIM/JIT for admin exceptions. summary: Your Dynamics 365 dashboards don’t “just work” everywhere—and that mismatch is killing trust. SharePoint page (Power BI web part) → Best for execs/board needing curated, print-friendly snapshots with light interactivity. Dataverse for Teams → Good for lightweight CRM tables in Teams; not for complex relationships or deep analytics. Dedicated Power BI app/workspace → Best for power users/analysts who need full interactivity, drill, and self-serve. What Breaks (and Why) 1) Data Freshness Teams: Can feel “live” (DirectQuery/short refresh), but every viewer needs the right license ; missing Pro/Viewer = blank tabs. SharePoint: Stable nightly refresh by default; great for scheduled reporting, not hour-by-hour ops. 2) Interactivity & Drill Teams: Strong for quick filters + comments; heavy drill can be clunky on mobile. SharePoint: Looks polished; some interactive features or exports may be limited depending on embed method and capacity. 3) Security & Access Different surfaces, same row-level security— but group membership, conditional access, or guest access can diverge → users see blanks with no clear error. SharePoint may push you toward Premium capacity for broad interactive viewing. Budget before rollout. 5) Mobile & Offline Reality Teams mobile: Great in coverage; fragile offline. SharePoint on tablet: Pretty snapshots; heavy drill on custom entities often fails. Field-first? Build a lite mobile report (small visuals, essential KPIs, minimal DAX).
